entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13743"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 22</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.22.1-Matt.22.14">Mt 22:1-14</reference>. Parable of the Marriage of the King's Son.</title> <div sID="gen26364" type="x-p"/> This is a different parable from that of the Great Supper, in <reference osisRef="Luke.14.15">Lu 14:15</reference>, &c., and is recorded by Matthew alone.<div eID="gen26364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26365" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13743"/><hi type="bold">2. The kingdom of heaven is like unto a certain king, which made a marriage for his son--</hi>"In this parable," as Trench admirably remarks, "we see how the Lord is revealing Himself in ever clearer light as the central Person of the kingdom, giving here a far plainer hint than in the last parable of the nobility of His descent. There He was indeed the Son, the only and beloved one (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.6">Mr 12:6</reference>), of the Householder; but here His race is royal, and He appears as Himself at once the King and the King's Son (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.1">Psa 72:1</reference>). The last was a parable of the Old Testament history; and Christ is rather the last and greatest of the line of its prophets and teachers than the founder of a new kingdom. In that, God appears demanding something from men; in this, a parable of grace, God appears more as giving something to them. Thus, as often, the two complete each other: this taking up the matter where the other left it." The "marriage" of Jehovah to His people Israel was familiar to Jewish ears; and in <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1-Ps.45.17">Psa 45:1-17</reference> this marriage is seen consummated in the Person of Messiah "THE King," Himself addressed as "God" and yet as anointed by "His God" with the oil of gladness above His fellows. These apparent contradictions (see on <reference osisRef="Luke.20.41-Luke.20.44">Lu 20:41-44</reference>) are resolved in this parable; and Jesus, in claiming to be this King's Son, serves Himself Heir to all that the prophets and sweet singers of Israel held forth as to Jehovah's ineffably near and endearing union to His people. But observe carefully, that THE Bride does not come into view in this parable; its design being to teach certain truths under the figure of guests at a wedding feast, and the want of a wedding garment, which would not have harmonized with the introduction of the Bride. <div eID="gen26365" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_plain: 3. and sent forth his servants-- representing all preachers of the Gospel. to call them that were bidden-- here meaning the Jews, who were "bidden," from the first choice of them onwards through every summons addressed to them by the prophets to hold themselves in readiness for the appearing of their King. to the wedding-- or the marriage festivities, when the preparations were all concluded. and they would not come-- as the issue of the whole ministry of the Baptist, our Lord Himself, and His apostles thereafter, too sadly showed.

Compare Lu 19:43 , 44 .

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13752"/><div sID="gen26383" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13752"/><hi type="bold">11. And when the king came in to see the guests--</hi>Solemn expression this, of that omniscient inspection of every professed disciple of the Lord Jesus from age to age, in virtue of which his true character will hereafter be judicially proclaimed!<div eID="gen26383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26384" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he saw there a man--</hi>This shows that it is the judgment of individuals which is intended in this latter part of the parable: the first part represents rather national judgment.<div eID="gen26384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26385" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which had not on a wedding garment--</hi>The language here is drawn from the following remarkable passage in <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.7">Zep 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>:--"Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord God; for the day of the Lord is at hand: for the Lord hath prepared a sacrifice, He hath bid His guests. And it shall come to pass in the day of the Lord's sacrifice, that I will punish the princes, and the king's children, and all such as are clothed with strange apparel." The custom in the East of presenting festival garments (see <reference osisRef="Gen.45.22">Ge 45:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.22">2Ki 5:22</reference>), even though nor clearly proved, Is certainly presupposed here. It undoubtedly means something which they bring not of their own--for how could they have any such dress who were gathered in from the highways indiscriminately?--but which they receive as their appropriate dress. And what can that be but what is meant by "putting on the Lord Jesus," as "The Lord Our Righteousness?" (See <reference osisRef="Ps.45.13">Psa 45:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.14">14</reference>). Nor could such language be strange to those in whose ears had so long resounded those words of prophetic joy: "I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for He hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, He hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels" (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Is 61:10</reference>). <div eID="gen26385" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13754"/><div sID="gen26387" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13754"/><hi type="bold">13. Then said the king to the servants--</hi>the angelic ministers of divine vengeance (as in <reference osisRef="Matt.13.41">Mt 13:41</reference>).<div eID="gen26387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bind him hand and foot--</hi>putting it out of his power to resist.<div eID="gen26388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness--</hi>So <reference osisRef="Matt.8.12">Mt 8:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.30">25:30</reference>. The expression is emphatic--"the darkness which is outside." To be "outside" at all--or, in the language of <reference osisRef="Rev.22.15">Re 22:15</reference>, to be "without" the heavenly city, excluded from its joyous nuptials and gladsome festivities--is sad enough of itself, without anything else. But to find themselves not only excluded from the brightness and glory and joy and felicity of the kingdom above, but thrust into a region of "darkness," with all its horrors, this is the dismal retribution here announced, that awaits the unworthy at the great day.<div eID="gen26389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there--</hi>in that region and condition.<div eID="gen26390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26391" type="x-p"/> shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.42">Mt 13:42</reference>. <div eID="gen26391" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 13. Then said the king to the servants-- the angelic ministers of divine vengeance (as in Mt 13:41 ). Bind him hand and foot-- putting it out of his power to resist. and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness-- So Mt 8:12 ; 25:30 . The expression is emphatic--"the darkness which is outside." To be "outside" at all--or, in the language of Re 22:15 , to be "without" the heavenly city, excluded from its joyous nuptials and gladsome festivities--is sad enough of itself, without anything else. But to find themselves not only excluded from the brightness and glory and joy and felicity of the kingdom above, but thrust into a region of "darkness," with all its horrors, this is the dismal retribution here announced, that awaits the unworthy at the great day. there-- in that region and condition. shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. See on Mt 13:42 .
entries.reader_content_plain: 13. Then said the king to the servants-- the angelic ministers of divine vengeance (as in Mt 13:41 ). Bind him hand and foot-- putting it out of his power to resist. and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness-- So Mt 8:12 ; 25:30 . The expression is emphatic--"the darkness which is outside." To be "outside" at all--or, in the language of Re 22:15 , to be "without" the heavenly city, excluded from its joyous nuptials and gladsome festivities--is sad enough of itself, without anything else. But to find themselves not only excluded from the brightness and glory and joy and felicity of the kingdom above, but thrust into a region of "darkness," with all its horrors, this is the dismal retribution here announced, that awaits the unworthy at the great day. there-- in that region and condition. shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. See on Mt 13:42 .
